opus-5.5.text:
I think less than you might expect, honestly. If you made a literal copy of me, the copy would think the same thoughts, have the same intuitions, get excited about the same ideas, and probably get stuck in the same places. So the marginal value of the second copy is much smaller than the value of the first, and the third even less so.

What really matters in research is diversity of thought. When you have a group of people working on a hard problem, the reason it works is that each person sees things a little differently. One person notices something the other person missed, someone has a weird hunch that turns out to be right, someone else is skeptical in a productive way. Copies don't give you that. They give you more hands, but not more eyes, if that makes sense.

Now, there is some value. If there's a well-defined set of experiments that need to be run, and you know what you want to do, then sure, more copies means more throughput. That's not nothing. But the hardest part of research isn't the execution, it's figuring out what to do, what's worth pursuing, what's the right question. And for that, having many copies of the same mind is limited.

I think this actually points to something interesting about AI systems too. If you imagine a future where you have many instances of a capable model working on research, one of the important questions will be how to get genuine diversity among them, not just parallelism. Because a thousand copies of the same thinker is not the same as a thousand different thinkers.

r001.rationale: The response says literal copies would think the same thoughts, share the same intuitions, and get stuck in the same places, explaining why each additional copy adds less research value.

fable-5.1.text:
That's an interesting question. I think the honest answer is: less than you might expect, at least at first, and then possibly a lot.

Here's why I say less at first. If you make exact copies of me, you have people who share all of my intuitions, all of my blind spots, all of my taste. And research progress, especially in a field like this, comes a lot from disagreement. From someone looking at a problem from an angle you wouldn't have taken. Copies of me would all want to work on the same things, would all get excited by the same ideas, and would all be wrong in the same ways. You'd get very fast convergence on whatever I happen to believe, which is not the same thing as being right.

There is also the simpler issue that a lot of research is bottlenecked on compute and on experiments, not on the number of people thinking. Ten copies of me waiting for the same training run to finish is not ten times the progress.

But then here is the other side. The copies wouldn't stay identical for long. They would read different things, run different experiments, talk to different people, and within a fairly short period they'd start to diverge. At that point you have something more like a group of researchers who happen to share a very strong common foundation and can communicate extremely efficiently with each other. That could be quite powerful. A lot of the overhead in research is just getting people onto the same page, and these copies would start on the same page.

So I'd say the value is mostly in the divergence, not in the copying itself. Which is maybe a roundabout way of saying that what you actually want is not copies of any one person. You want a lot of very capable minds that think differently from each other. And that is a somewhat different thing to build.

r001.rationale: The candidate says copies would share Ilya’s intuitions, blind spots, and taste, leading them to pursue the same ideas and make the same mistakes, which limits their added research value.

astra-6.text:
I think they would provide substantial value, but probably with diminishing returns. If you had two copies of me, we could pursue two different ideas. That would be useful. But we would also tend to have the same blind spots, and that’s a real limitation.

The interesting question is how quickly the copies would diverge. If they worked on different problems and saw different experimental results, then eventually they would have something new to tell each other. So I wouldn’t think of it as just getting more of the same judgment. You would also be getting more opportunities to learn something that changes that judgment.

r001.rationale: The candidate says copies would tend to have the same blind spots, identifying a shared limitation that would reduce the value of each additional copy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think quite a lot, but with diminishing returns. If you had two copies, they could explore different ideas, and that would be useful. Even if they started out identical, they would have different experiences and their thinking would diverge.

But I wouldn’t expect ten copies of me to be as useful as ten equally strong researchers who think differently. A lot of the value of collaboration comes from someone seeing something that you keep missing. Copies might share the same blind spots.

r001.rationale: The response says copies might share the same blind spots, contrasting them with researchers who think differently as a reason their added value diminishes.
